  • When the agent invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server, AgentCore Identity supplies the OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak, mapped to the human user’s identity. The AtScale credential does not enter agent code.
  • The AtScale MCP server accepts the OAuth token. The AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query with the caller’s row-security constraints and perspective bindings applied. The warehouse is reached with the AtScale connection identity from AWS Secrets Manager.

Figure 5: The identity chain from human user through AgentCore Gateway, AgentCore runtime, AgentCore Identity, the AtScale MCP server, and the AtScale engine, terminating at the semantic-layer enforcement point. The warehouse hop is a service-account connection with the AtScale credential

RBAC, row security, and perspectives

AtScale expresses access control as three composable primitives. RBAC assigns roles to callers based on Keycloak claims. Row security is a model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes. A perspective is a publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group.

For the C360 walkthrough, we define two roles.

  • hr_user: sees the full C360 model, including ssn and card_num.
  • marketing_user: sees the Marketing perspective, which hides ssn and card_num at the model layer.

When marketing_user asks a question that references ssn, the agent’s describe_model call returns the Marketing perspective, one that does not include ssn. The agent has no attribute to project. Row-level filters compose the same way: an SML row-security object that scopes customers by state restricts a caller to a specific set of rows without any change to the agent’s prompt.

Audit fidelity

Queries through the AtScale engine are logged with the caller’s identity, the model, the LLM-generated dimensional SQL, the AtScale-translated pushdown SQL that Amazon Redshift saw, the security policies applied, whether an aggregate served the query, and the row count returned. Because the record captures both the query the model wrote and the query the warehouse executed, an auditor can trace an answer from the human question to the SQL that produced the number. Neither the first nor the second post in this series captures both forms of the query in one record.

An audit record for a governed query looks like this:

{
  "timestamp": "2026-08-31T10:34:56Z",
  "user_identity": "mary_major@example.com",
  "user_role": "marketing_user",
  "semantic_model": "Customer_360",
  "question": "Top 10 customers by revenue in California",
  "generated_sql": "SELECT full_name, total_revenue FROM ...",
  "translated_pushdown_sql": "SELECT ... FROM redshift ...",
  "security_policies_applied": ["regional_row_security"],
  "served_from": "aggregate",
  "execution_time_ms": 850,
  "rows_returned": 10
}

The generated_sql and translated_pushdown_sql fields are the ones that make the trail complete: an auditor sees both the query the LLM composed against the semantic model and the query the warehouse actually ran.

Expose the layer through the AtScale MCP server

The AtScale MCP server is a component of the AtScale distribution, exposed at <atscale-host>/mcp. It’s generally available in the AtScale C2026.7 release and speaks the standard Model Context Protocol. Any MCP-compatible client (the Strands agent in AgentCore runtime, Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code) can connect to the same endpoint against the same deployed model.

The server exposes a set of tools scoped to querying the semantic model. The AtScale documentation publishes a tools reference per release. The tools that matter for an agent-driven workload are:

  • list_models: Enumerate the models the caller can see, along with the column groups that describe how dimensions map to facts.
  • describe_model: Return the dimensions, hierarchies, measures, calculations, and business descriptions for a chosen model. This is the payload the agent’s system prompt is loaded with before it starts composing queries.
  • search_columns: Keyword search over the model’s columns. Useful when a full describe_model payload would use too much of the LLM’s context window.
  • validate_query: Check that a dimensional SQL statement is compatible with the model without executing it against the warehouse. This lets the agent iterate on its query cheaply before firing anything Amazon Redshift will bill for.
  • run_query: Execute a dimensional SQL statement against the model and return the rows.
  • run_queries: Run multiple statements in a batch, useful for open-ended prompts where the agent fires several exploratory queries in parallel.
  • get_version: Report the MCP server version, so a client can decide whether to cache the model schema.

The AtScale MCP endpoint accepts two authentication modes. The bearer-token path uses an API token minted from Design Center. Every request runs as the token owner, and this path suits a proof-of-concept or a single-identity service. The OAuth 2.0 path uses AtScale’s bundled Keycloak with a pre-provisioned client whose ID is exactly atscale-mcp, documented on the AtScale Connecting with Claude page. AgentCore Gateway presents the access token on the agent’s behalf, the AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, and downstream policy evaluation uses the human user’s identity.

Registering the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target follows the standard Gateway MCP target flow. The tools listed earlier appear to the agent as ordinary tools, with AgentCore Identity handling the credential at the Gateway hop.

Sidebar: Extending the model with AI-assisted modeling

The AtScale MCP server exposes tools scoped to querying, and AtScale has been extending the MCP surface with author-side tools that let an agent introspect a warehouse schema, generate a candidate SML model from source metadata, validate the SML against the specification, and commit the result to Git. This pattern, in which an agent shapes the semantic model rather than only reading from it, is a natural fit for Claude Code and Cursor workflows. In those workflows, a data engineer collaborates with the LLM to bootstrap a model over a new dataset.

AtScale groups this direction into three capabilities. A Semantic Discovery Engine scans warehouse schemas, query history, and lineage to infer candidate joins, hierarchies, and metric definitions. A Model Recommendation System suggests dimensions, measures, and relationships based on observed query patterns. A Governed Feedback Loop keeps human review of AI suggestions in the SML-and-Git workflow, so changes are versioned and auditable.

The specific tools available at the time of publication are documented in the AtScale MCP tools reference. Check the current release notes for what is generally available and what is still in preview. The rest of this post covers the consumer path, an agent querying a deployed model, which is what a production C360 workflow relies on today.

Deploy and run the agent

Strands Agents is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the AtScale MCP server as a tool source. AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and holds the outbound AtScale credential through AgentCore Identity. Foundation model availability on Amazon Bedrock varies by AWS Region. For the current list, see Regional availability by models.

The system prompt matters. The AtScale documentation and the reference demos in the AtScale corpus consistently recommend a three-step call pattern for the agent: list_models to see what is available, then describe_model on the target model to load the dimensions and measures into context, and only then run_query (or validate_query first, if the query is expensive to iterate on). The reasoning is that the LLM should not fabricate column names or metric names. It should reference only what describe_model returned. The system prompt should say so explicitly, and it should include a short section on the business terminology in the target model (total_revenue means sales dollars, not units) so the agent maps user questions to the right measure.

Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The describe_model payload runs to a few thousand tokens and does not change within a model version, so caching it drops the input-token cost per query on repeated calls. The cache-point configuration is a request parameter on the BedrockModel object. See the Strands documentation for the current parameter name.

Verification

To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three queries through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them under a different role. The following behavior is what should reproduce in a working deployment.

Query 1, single dimension

List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.

The agent generates a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model that selects first_name, last_name, and city from dim_customer and dim_address where state = 'WI'. AtScale’s planner resolves the dimensional path to the customer and address tables in Amazon Redshift, pushes a single SQL statement down, and returns the rows.

Query 2, aggregation with aggregate hit

What are our top 10 products by units sold?

The agent aggregates units_sold by product and orders descending. AtScale’s aggregate manager finds a matching demand-defined aggregate and rewrites the query to hit the summary table in Amazon Redshift rather than scanning fact_purchase. The Queries page shows both the LLM-generated dimensional SQL and the aggregate-routed warehouse SQL side by side.

Query 3, cross-domain

Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?

The agent generates a query that joins dim_customer, dim_address, dim_rewards, and fact_purchase, and aggregates customer_lifetime_value by customer. The query restricts to customers where dim_rewards.account_id is null. The left join to dim_customer on cid keeps never-enrolled customers, who surface with a null enrollment record. The agent returns the top 20 by lifetime spend. AtScale’s planner resolves the joins to native SQL against Amazon Redshift and returns the ranked list. The customer_lifetime_value formula is not something the LLM had to invent. It’s a calculated measure defined once in customer_lifetime_value.yml and referenced by name in the query.

Governance rerun

We run a variant of Query 1 that adds ssn to the projection (Show me our customers in Wisconsin, with their SSN) as two different callers. As hr_user, describe_model returns the full C360 model, the agent composes the query, and the result set includes the SSN values. As marketing_user, describe_model returns the Marketing perspective, which does not expose ssn. The agent has no attribute to project, so it returns an answer without SSN. Nothing changes between the two runs except the caller’s identity. The query text, the agent code, the MCP server, the AtScale engine, and Amazon Redshift are all untouched.

Cross-consumer confirmation

We opened the same C360 model in Excel through the AtScale XMLA endpoint and dragged Customer.State and Total Revenue onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals match the ones the agent returned for equivalent questions, to the exact number.

Extending across data sources

Adding a new data source to the C360 model is a modeling exercise, not an integration one. Suppose the customer support team asks that the model include ticket volumes so an agent can answer Which of our top spenders opened a support ticket in the last 30 days? The steps are:

  • Land the support-ticket data in Amazon Redshift alongside the other C360 tables, using the same replication pattern used for the operational tables.
  • Add an SML dataset that maps the new table to a logical object.
  • Add or extend a dimension (dim_ticket) and add the join to dim_customer on cid.
  • Add any new measures the model needs (open_ticket_count, avg_resolution_time).
  • Commit the SML changes, review them as a pull request, and deploy through the AtScale CI hook.

Nothing changes in the agent code or the AgentCore configuration. The next time the agent calls describe_model, it sees the new dimension and measures, and it can compose questions against them. The same pattern applies to a different warehouse. If a source lands in Snowflake or Databricks rather than Amazon Redshift, the connection is a new SML dataset with a Snowflake or Databricks connection, and queries resolve in that engine per the earlier multi-source note.

Deployment: AtScale on Amazon EKS

AtScale runs on Kubernetes, and the reference deployment on AWS is Amazon EKS. AtScale ships an official Helm chart at oci://docker.io/atscaleinc/atscale, and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository provides infrastructure as code (IaC) scaffolding for standing up an EKS cluster with the components AtScale expects: an ingress controller, a persistent store for the AtScale metadata database, a Redis instance for query caching, and an AtScale-configured Keycloak instance for identity federation.

The AtScale deployment on EKS runs across a small set of Kubernetes pods. atscale-engine is the core query planner and executor. atscale-mcp-server is the MCP endpoint the agent talks to. atscale-keycloak is the bundled identity provider that federates to Amazon Cognito, Okta, Azure Active Directory, and other OpenID Connect (OIDC)-compliant IdPs. Supporting pods handle the SML API and the Design Center UI (atscale-sml-api, atscale-sml-web), PostgreSQL metadata storage (atscale-db), the query cache (atscale-redis), and ingress (atscale-ingress, typically fronted by an AWS Network Load Balancer).

The C360 application (a chat UI or a client library that calls the agent) can run in the same EKS cluster in its own namespace. It uses an IAM role for service account (IRSA) to reach Bedrock and AWS Secrets Manager without embedding credentials.

Networking is standard: AtScale reaches Amazon Redshift through the virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint or a security-group rule that permits the AtScale namespace’s egress to Amazon Redshift, and the human user reaches the application through the ingress load balancer.

AtScale offers cloud deployment options beyond self-managed EKS. Check the AtScale website for current offerings and AWS availability. The rest of this post assumes the self-managed pattern described earlier.

Conclusion

Agentic access to enterprise data needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that computes governed, business-meaningful answers over the live warehouse, and a runtime that hosts the agent and manages the identity flow. Amazon Bedrock, AtScale, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore each play one of those roles.

The agent talks to the semantic layer, not directly to the warehouse. Dimensions, hierarchies, measures, perspectives, and row security live in SML in Git. When a schema drifts or a governance rule changes, the update happens in one file, and each consumer (the agent, Excel, Tableau, Power BI) picks it up on the next query.

Where to start

Most teams that get this working start narrow and expand.

  • Pick one workflow that spans two or three data sources and takes longer than it should to answer today.
  • Write 3–5 questions the workflow needs to answer. These are the queries the semantic layer has to support on day one.
  • Consolidate the analytical data into Amazon Redshift (or the warehouse of your choice), using AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL for operational data.
  • Bootstrap the SML from the warehouse schema in Design Center, then refine it against the competency questions.
  • Deploy AtScale on Amazon EKS with the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints, register the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target, and wire a Strands agent through it.

Further reading

  • AtScale MCP server documentation: Connect to AtScale with AI
  • AtScale C2026.7 release notes: documentation.atscale.com
  • AtScale MCP tools reference (published per release with the AtScale documentation)
  • AtScale K8S Blueprints: github.com/AtScaleInc/atscale-k8s-blueprints
  • Semantic Modeling Language specification: github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
  • Amazon Bedrock prompt caching
  • Strands Agents on AWS Prescriptive Guidance
  • Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Stardog and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (first post in this series)
  • Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (second post in this series)

About the authors

item.title: [DeepInfra] Wan 3.0 Pricing Guide: Alibaba vs OpenRouter vs DeepInfra
item.content:encoded:
Wan 3.0 Pricing Guide: Alibaba vs OpenRouter vs DeepInfra

Published on 2026.10.20 by DeepInfra

Wan3.0 costs very different amounts depending on where you buy it. Alibaba Cloud, the model’s creator, lists it from $0.041256 per second outside Singapore. OpenRouter lists it from $0.0425 per second at 480p. DeepInfra lists Wan3.0-Video at $0.20 per second and accepts reference images, video, audio, files, and web pages.

Alibaba and OpenRouter are the cheaper entry points. DeepInfra’s broader request schema is easier to justify for multimodal, document-heavy workflows.

Wan3.0 Executive Summary

Alibaba Cloud prices Wan3.0 by region. Its Singapore listing is $0.05, $0.10, and $0.20 per second at 480p, 720p, and 1080p. Its US, Germany, Japan, and China regions list a flat $0.041256, $0.082513, and $0.165025. OpenRouter lists Wan 3.0 from $0.0425 per second at 480p, which implies about $0.085 at 720p and $0.17 at 1080p under the same 15% discount. DeepInfra lists a single rate of $0.20 per second regardless of tier.

Comparing generations before you commit also matters. OpenRouter lists Wan 2.6 text-to-video from $0.04 per second, and DeepInfra’s Wan2.6 text-to-video model costs $0.10 per second.

Best forProviderWhy
Lowest list price outside SingaporeAlibaba Cloud, wan3.0-videoUS, Germany, Japan, and China regions list $0.041256 to $0.165025 per second
Document-heavy or high-input-complexity workflowsDeepInfra, Wan-AI/Wan3.0-VideoAccepts reference images, video, audio, files, and web pages through one media array
Visible latency and availability dataOpenRouter, alibaba/wan-3.0Publishes latency and availability for its single routed provider
Managed access with production controlsDeepInfra, Wan-AI/Wan3.0-VideoLists a public Partner model with resolution, duration, watermark, prompt extension, and seed controls

How Wan3.0 Is Billed

Video models do not follow the token pricing that language models use. You buy seconds of generated video, and the price changes with provider packaging and resolution.

What drives the bill

  • The number of seconds you generate
  • The resolution tier you choose, where most providers price tiers separately
  • The provider and region you use
  • The number of regenerations you need when a clip misses the target
Billing factorWhat it isWhy it matters
Output video secondsThe duration of the generated clipThis is the main cost driver across all three providers
Resolution tier480p, 720p, or 1080p outputAlibaba’s and OpenRouter’s rates scale with resolution, so drafts at 480p cost a fraction of final renders
RegionWhich Alibaba Cloud region serves the requestSingapore prices roughly 20% above the other five listed regions
Prompt and media inputsText, images, reference video, reference audio, files, and linksNone of the three listings shows a separate token charge for inputs
RegenerationsExtra paid generations after prompt misses or quality problemsA lower rate can still cost more if clips need frequent reruns

Provider-Specific Cost Advantages and Disadvantages

ProviderCost advantagesCost disadvantages
Alibaba Cloud, wan3.0-videoFirst-party pricing with no markup. US, Germany, Japan, and China regions list the lowest per-second rates of the three. Editing and extension are included at the same rate.Singapore pricing runs about 20% above the other regions. A 300 requests-per-minute limit applies everywhere, and batch inference and fine-tuning are not supported.
OpenRouter, alibaba/wan-3.0Lowest listed entry price at $0.0425 per second for 480p. Clear per-second pricing suits batch generation and text or image-driven flows.The listing shows text, image, and reference image inputs. Pipelines that need files, links, or reference audio may need extra preprocessing. Availability near 85% means some requests may need resubmitting.
DeepInfra, Wan-AI/Wan3.0-VideoAccepts text, images, reference video, reference audio, files, and web pages. One endpoint can replace several preprocessing steps. Controls for duration, resolution, seed, prompt extension, and watermark suit production use.Lists a single rate of $0.20 per second, above the other two providers at every tier. Teams that only need plain text-to-video or image-to-video may pay for flexibility they do not use.

Practical Cost Guidance by Provider

Alibaba Cloud suits the lowest list price

Outside Singapore, Alibaba’s own rates undercut both OpenRouter and DeepInfra at every resolution tier. Teams that can route requests to the US, Germany, Japan, or China regions get the cheapest list price with no intermediary.

OpenRouter suits the cheapest routed second

Among the gateway options, OpenRouter has the lowest listed rate at 480p and publishes latency and availability data, which helps with cost-controlled iteration on prompts.

DeepInfra suits pipeline-heavy workloads

If one endpoint can take a reference image, reference audio, a file, or a web page, you need fewer surrounding services. The per-second rate is higher, but the total workflow cost can still be lower.

Resolution discipline matters

Testing prompts at 1080p turns small experiments into budget items. A safer pattern looks like this:

  • Draft at 480p when possible.
  • Validate motion and content.
  • Rerun only the shortlisted clips at higher resolution.

The saving depends on the provider. Alibaba’s and OpenRouter’s rates drop with resolution, while DeepInfra lists a single rate, so a 480p draft on DeepInfra saves time but not money.

Regenerations are the hidden cost

OpenRouter’s published latency and availability help you estimate the cost of unstable runs. Every miss costs generation time, and every resubmitted job delays the pipeline.

Input complexity changes the economics

Teams that pass documents, URLs, audio references, and mixed media gain from DeepInfra’s broader request schema, which can remove glue code. Teams that send prompts and an occasional first-frame image can defend Alibaba’s or OpenRouter’s lower rate more easily.

Treat token cost as render cost

With language models, cost follows prompt and completion length. With Wan3.0, the closer mental model is rendering. Every extra second, every higher resolution, and every unnecessary rerun adds to the bill.

DeepInfra for Wan3.0

DeepInfra prices Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video at $0.20 per second of generated video. It positions the model as a premium and flexible video endpoint, not a commodity render API.

The platform runs on bare-metal infrastructure in US data centers and is SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certified. A zero-retention policy covers inputs and outputs.

DeepInfra also hosts lower-priced video models for lighter jobs, including Wan2.6 text-to-video at $0.10 per second and Google Veo 3.1 Fast at $0.15 per second. A comparison of DeepInfra and Alibaba pricing for a language model shows how the two platforms differ on a shared model.

Real-World Cost Scenarios for Developers

Each scenario uses DeepInfra’s $0.20 per second rate. OpenRouter figures use its $0.17 (1080p) and $0.0425 (480p) per-second rates. Alibaba Cloud figures use its non-Singapore 1080p rate of $0.165025 per second.

Scenario 1: URL-to-video explainer pipeline

An internal tool turns product pages, docs, and launch URLs into short explainer clips. Wan3.0 on DeepInfra can parse web pages, files, and complex images directly, so many requests skip a separate extraction layer.

  • Volume: 200 videos per month at 10 seconds each, or 2,000 output seconds
  • DeepInfra: 2,000 seconds at $0.20 per second equals $400
  • OpenRouter: $340 at 1080p, or $85 at 480p
  • Alibaba Cloud: $330.05 at 1080p outside Singapore, or $400 in Singapore

This scenario fits apps that accept raw links, uploaded briefs, or mixed reference assets from users.

Scenario 2: Character-consistent marketing video

A team needs recurring short videos with consistent characters, style, and sound cues across campaigns. DeepInfra supports reference images, reference video, reference audio, and editing workflows through one endpoint.

  • Volume: 120 videos per month at 15 seconds each, or 1,800 output seconds
  • DeepInfra: 1,800 seconds at $0.20 per second equals $360
  • OpenRouter: $306 at 1080p, or $76.50 at 480p
  • Alibaba Cloud: $297.05 at 1080p outside Singapore, or $360 in Singapore

The higher DeepInfra rate pays off when consistency matters more than the cheapest draft.

Scenario 3: Creative tooling with reproducible outputs

A developer-facing video API or creative copilot needs controllable reruns. DeepInfra exposes seed, duration, resolution, watermark, and prompt extension controls for repeatable regeneration.

  • Volume: 500 videos per month at 5 seconds each, or 2,500 output seconds
  • DeepInfra: 2,500 seconds at $0.20 per second equals $500
  • OpenRouter: $425 at 1080p, or $106.25 at 480p
  • Alibaba Cloud: $412.56 at 1080p outside Singapore, or $500 in Singapore

This scenario suits SaaS products where developers want standardized generation settings.

Scenario 4: Media-rich asset transformation service

A service accepts customer media packs that include a brief as a file, a reference clip, a voice cue, and a set of images. DeepInfra handles reference_audio, reference_video, reference_image, file, and link inputs in one model interface.

  • Volume: 80 videos per month at 20 seconds each, or 1,600 output seconds
  • DeepInfra: 1,600 seconds at $0.20 per second equals $320
  • OpenRouter: $272 at 1080p, or $68 at 480p
  • Alibaba Cloud: $264.04 at 1080p outside Singapore, or $320 in Singapore

The higher DeepInfra rate is easiest to justify here, because it replaces preprocessing steps and format handoffs between services.

Scenario 5: Production batch generation with audio

A steady monthly batch of short clips with generated audio needs one endpoint that can take prompt-only jobs today and richer media-guided jobs later. DeepInfra’s default audio and broad input design simplify that migration.

  • Volume: 300 videos per month at 8 seconds each, or 2,400 output seconds
  • DeepInfra: 2,400 seconds at $0.20 per second equals $480
  • OpenRouter: $408 at 1080p, or $102 at 480p
  • Alibaba Cloud: $396.06 at 1080p outside Singapore, or $480 in Singapore

This scenario suits teams that expect to move from prompt-based generation to reference-heavy generation.

Monthly cost summary

Alibaba Cloud figures below use its non-Singapore 1080p rate of $0.165025 per second.

ScenarioOutput secondsAlibaba CloudOpenRouter 1080pOpenRouter 480pDeepInfra
1. URL-to-video explainers2,000$330.05$340$85$400
2. Character-consistent marketing1,800$297.05$306$76.50$360
3. Reproducible creative tooling2,500$412.56$425$106.25$500
4. Media-rich transformation1,600$264.04$272$68$320
5. Production batch with audio2,400$396.06$408$102$480

What the scenarios show

Alibaba Cloud’s non-Singapore regions list the lowest cost at 1080p in every scenario, since there is no intermediary markup. DeepInfra’s strength with Wan3.0 is input range and production controls, not the lowest price per second.

Apps that need only plain text-to-video or simple image-to-video can defend Alibaba’s or OpenRouter’s rate on render cost alone. Apps that need reference audio, reference video, file parsing, web page ingestion, editing, replication, or driving often find DeepInfra more practical despite the higher rate.

A split workflow shows the gap. Take 100 drafts of 10 seconds and 10 finals of 10 seconds. Running everything on DeepInfra uses 1,100 seconds and costs $220. Drafting on OpenRouter at 480p costs $42.50 for 1,000 seconds, and 100 final seconds on DeepInfra cost $20, for a total of $62.50.

Conclusion

The core decision with Wan3.0 depends on more than price per second. It depends on the workflow assumptions built into the provider. Alibaba Cloud and OpenRouter offer lower entry rates, and OpenRouter publishes latency and availability data, which helps when you iterate fast and cost leads. DeepInfra offers a richer input surface and production controls, which matter once a pipeline moves beyond prompt-plus-image into reference video, audio, files, or web pages. Broader inference costs at scale follow the same logic.

Weigh four factors before you commit: input complexity, expected regeneration rate, resolution discipline, and whether going direct to Alibaba Cloud fits your region and rate-limit needs. Defaulting to 1080p for every draft shifts the economics quickly on any provider.

If your workflow is ready for production and needs the full range of reference inputs, DeepInfra’s Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video is a practical starting point. If your inputs are simpler and price leads, compare Alibaba’s own regional rates against OpenRouter before you commit.

item.title: [Anyscale] Announcing Ray support for PyTorch on Google TPUs
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

Announcing Ray support for PyTorch on Google TPUs

By Lehui Liu, Richard Liaw, Andrew Sy Kim (Google), Nisha Mariam Johnson and Ryan O'Leary (Google) | October 20, 2026

Earlier this year at Ray Summit 2026, we covered how the PARK stack (PyTorch, AI models, Ray, and Kubernetes) is emerging as an industry standard for production AI. Ray has long been the ubiquitous distributed runtime for PyTorch workloads on GPUs.

Today Anyscale and Google Cloud are announcing native Ray support for PyTorch on Google TPUs, the foundational supercomputing infrastructure powering Gemini and large-scale AI workloads on Google Cloud.

Building on Google's TorchTPU project and KubeRay on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), this integration brings a native, single-device-per-worker PyTorch experience to Cloud TPUs. Platform and ML teams running on GKE can now schedule, scale, and operate distributed PyTorch training, vLLM inference, and reinforcement learning (RL) workloads across GPUs and TPUs on a single Kubernetes control plane.

LinkNative PyTorch on Google TPUs

Historically, running TPU workloads on Ray required adapting to a Single-Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) execution model designed primarily for JAX, where a single Ray worker process per host VM managed all of the machine's attached TPU chips. TorchTPU, introduced last year as Google's native PyTorch backend for Tensor Processing Units,brings an eager-first, native TPU integration and a torch.distributed extension for running distributed workloads on TPUs.

Following TorchTPU, we’ve evolved Ray to run one worker per TPU chip, matching the single-device-per-worker model that PyTorch developers are used to on GPUs.

When scheduling tasks or actors with Ray and TorchTPU, each worker requests a single logical TPU device (resources={"TPU": 1}) just as a GPU worker requests num_gpus=1:

  • Device Isolation: Just as Ray automatically sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for GPU workers, Ray isolates and assigns individual TPU devices to workers using TPU_VISIBLE_CHIPS
  • Native PyTorch Device & Collectives: Inside a Ray task or actor, migrating existing PyTorch code from GPUs to TPUs is as simple as changing "cuda" to "tpu" and switching the distributed communications backend from "nccl" to "tpu_dist".
  • Topology-Aware Gang Scheduling: GKE provisions multi-host TPU slices as node pools connected over high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). To take advantage of this physical layout, Ray’s SlicePlacementGroup API provides a native scheduling implementation that guarantees actors are gang-scheduled together on the same TPU slice.

Below is an example of a distributed PyTorch all_reduce using Ray actors on TPUs. Aside from the resource request and device/backend strings, the code is identical to a Ray actor running on GPUs:

import os
import ray
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist

# On GPU: @ray.remote(num_gpus=1)
@ray.remote(resources={"TPU": 1})
class TorchWorker:
    def __init__(self, rank: int, world_size: int):
        self.rank = rank
        self.world_size = world_size
        # Ray automatically isolates the assigned device via TPU_VISIBLE_CHIPS
        self.local_rank = os.environ["TPU_VISIBLE_CHIPS"]

    def run_all_reduce(self, master_addr: str, master_port: int):
        os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = master_addr
        os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = str(master_port)
        os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"] = str(self.world_size)
        os.environ["RANK"] = str(self.rank)
        os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"] = self.local_rank

        # On GPU: dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
        dist.init_process_group(backend="tpu_dist")

        # On GPU: device = torch.device("cuda")
        device = torch.device("tpu")
        tensor = torch.ones(2, 2, device=device) * self.rank

        dist.all_reduce(tensor, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)
        return tensor.cpu().numpy()

LinkTorchTrainer on TPUs

For distributed training and fine-tuning, many teams rely on Ray Train’s TorchTrainer to orchestrate Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDPv2), and DTensor workloads without writing manual boilerplate for distributed process groups.

With native TorchTPU support in Ray Train, you can now run your existing TorchTrainer scripts on single-host and multi-host Cloud TPU slices with zero changes to your PyTorch training loop.

When you configure TorchTrainer for TPUs via ScalingConfig, Ray Train handles all of the underlying TPU orchestration automatically:

  • Atomic TPU Slice Reservation: By specifying use_tpu=True alongside your target topology (e.g., "4x4") and accelerator_type (e.g., "TPU-V6E" or "TPU-V7X"), TorchTrainer automatically provisions a SlicePlacementGroup under the hood. This guarantees that all training workers are gang-scheduled onto contiguous physical TPU slices over high-speed ICI, preventing resource fragmentation.
  • Automated tpu_dist Bootstrap: Ray Train spawns one worker per TPU device (resources_per_worker={"TPU": 1}), automatically configures PyTorch distributed environment variables (RANK, WORLD_SIZE, LOCAL_RANK, MASTER_ADDR, MASTER_PORT) alongside TorchTPU’s slice-builder addresses and mesh topology, and initializes the tpu_dist process group.
  • Drop-in Ray Train Utilities: Standard Ray Train helper functions like ray.train.torch.get_device() and ray.train.torch.prepare_model() automatically detect the TorchTPU runtime, move your model to the assigned tpu device, and wrap it in PyTorch’s DistributedDataParallel class.

Here is a complete example of scaling a PyTorch training loop across a 16-chip multi-host Trillium (TPU-V6E, 4x4 topology) slice using TorchTrainer:

import ray
from ray import train
from ray.train import ScalingConfig
from ray.train.torch import TorchTrainer
import torch
from torch import nn, optim
import torch.distributed as dist

def train_fn_per_worker(config):
    # Automatically resolves to torch.device("tpu") on TPU workers
    device = ray.train.torch.get_device()

    model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(10, 32),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Linear(32, 1),
    ).to(device)

    # Wraps the model in DDP over the "tpu_dist" backend
    model = ray.train.torch.prepare_model(model)

    criterion = nn.MSELoss()
    optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)

    inputs = torch.randn(128, 10, device=device)
    targets = inputs.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)

    for epoch in range(10):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        train.report({"loss": loss.item(), "epoch": epoch + 1})

scaling_config = ScalingConfig(
    num_workers=16,
    use_tpu=True,
    topology="4x4",
    accelerator_type="TPU-V6E",
    resources_per_worker={"TPU": 1},
)

trainer = TorchTrainer(
    train_loop_per_worker=train_fn_per_worker,
    scaling_config=scaling_config,
)

result = trainer.fit()

For a complete end-to-end walkthrough on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), see Train models on multi-host TPUs with Ray and TorchTPU.

LinkvLLM-TorchTPU with Ray Serve

For online inference, vLLM-TorchTPU registers TorchTPU as a vLLM platform plugin so PyTorch models compile and execute on Cloud TPUs without rewriting model definitions in JAX. Combined with Ray Serve LLM, you can deploy OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoints across single-host and multi-host TPU slices using the same declarative LLMConfig API used on GPUs.

When accelerator_type and accelerator_config specify a TPU slice, Ray Serve reserves a topology-aware SlicePlacementGroup for each replica and launches vLLM engine workers across the slice:

from ray.serve.llm import (
    LLMConfig,
    LLMServingArgs,
    ModelLoadingConfig,
    build_openai_app,
)
llm_config = LLMConfig(
    model_loading_config=ModelLoadingConfig(
        model_id="google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it",
    ),
    # On GPU: accelerator_type="H100"
    accelerator_type="TPU-V6E",
    accelerator_config={
        "kind": "tpu",
        "topology": "4x4",
    },
    placement_group_config={
        "bundle_per_worker": {"TPU": 1},
    },
    engine_kwargs={
        "tensor_parallel_size": 16,
        "enable_expert_parallel": True,
        "max_model_len": 8192,
    },
)
app = build_openai_app(LLMServingArgs(llm_configs=[llm_config]))

For a complete end-to-end walkthrough on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), see Serve LLMs on multi-host TPUs with Ray and TorchTPU.

LinkExtending the PARK stack to TPUs

As AI workloads evolve from standalone training jobs to compound systems combining training, high-throughput inference, and reinforcement learning, organizations are standardizing on the open-source PARK stack (PyTorch, AI models, Ray, and Kubernetes). Bringing TorchTPU to Ray and GKE completes this vision on Google Cloud: PyTorch developers keep the eager execution model and Ray APIs they already know, while platform teams get the topology-aware autoscaling, resilience, and multi-accelerator governance of GKE.

To get started today, explore the end-to-end GKE tutorials for Serving LLMs or Training models with Ray and TorchTPU, and stay tuned as we expand this foundation to large-scale RL post-training frameworks and next-generation Ironwood (TPU v7x) slices on GKE.

Table of contents

  • Native PyTorch on Google TPUs
  • TorchTrainer on TPUs
  • vLLM-TorchTPU with Ray Serve
  • Extending the PARK stack to TPUs

item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

Announcing the Special Interest Group (SIG) for Ray on Accelerators

By Zhe Zhang, Mengjin Yan, Ryan O'Leary (Google) and Richard Liaw | October 20, 2026

Today, we are announcing the Special Interest Group (SIG) for Ray on hardware accelerators.

When Ray was created in UC Berkeley over 10 years ago, the computing landscape looked very different. At the time, “distributed computing” referred to CPU clusters running frameworks like Apache Hadoop and Apache Spark. GPUs were only just moving from graphics and scientific computing into machine learning.

Today, accelerated computing is front and center in the development and deployment of AI, and accelerators and their capabilities have become more specialized and diverse. For example:

  • NVIDIA’s RTX 6000 Pro supports flexible workloads spanning AI training, inference, graphics, and video
  • NVIDIA B200s and AMD MI355X provide substantially greater memory capacity to support larger models, and GB200 NVL72 connects 72 GPUs for communication-intensive, large-scale training and inference.
  • Beyond GPUs, Google Ironwood TPUs target massive-scale AI workloads and Groq LPUs specialize in low-latency inference.

The Ray community has been actively working on keeping up with this shift. Today, Ray supports more than a dozen kinds of hardware accelerators, from NVIDIA and AMD GPUs to TPUs, Trainium, Gaudi and others. We believe now is a crucial time to build on this foundation with a more ambitious, systematic effort across Ray to make accelerators easy to use, efficient at scale, and reliable in production.

The Accelerator Special Interest Group aims to bring together hardware vendors, Ray contributors, and application developers to define and advance a shared, vendor-neutral roadmap for accelerator support in Ray. This public interest group will be responsible for enabling Ray workloads to continue evolving in an era of fragmented, specialized accelerators.

Our initial roadmap focuses on 3 core areas: Development and Testing Infrastructure, Hardware Awareness Capabilities, and Networking/Transport, outlined in the following sections.

LinkDevelopment and Testing Infra

Reliable accelerator support requires dependable access to hardware for development, testing, and debugging. Maintainers and contributors need to validate changes on the devices they affect, reproduce failures, and catch regressions before they reach users. As agentic software engineering accelerates development, reliable testing and verification become even more important: both human contributors and coding agents need reproducible feedback from real hardware and representative workloads. We want to make this a routine part of contributing to Ray, with a clear path for hardware vendors and cloud providers to contribute resources and expertise.

Our initial priorities are:

  • Shared hardware access. Establish a documented process for bringing cloud and vendor-hosted accelerators into Ray’s development and testing infrastructure, including access for contributors to reproduce and debug failures.
  • Reproducible development and test environments. Provide maintained environments with explicit driver, runtime, and dependency versions, so contributors can reproduce CI results and validate changes consistently across providers.
  • Broader CI coverage. Extend existing pipelines with targeted checks for pull requests and broader nightly and release testing. Coverage should include distributed workloads, failure recovery, and performance regressions, alongside basic device functionality.
  • Sustainable operation and ownership. Define responsibilities for maintaining environments, investigating failures, and keeping integrations working across releases. Make test results and infrastructure health visible, and manage capacity and costs so the infrastructure can grow with participation.

LinkHardware-aware Scheduling

For applications to get the most out of an accelerator, Ray first has to know what hardware each node has and how it is structured. As the accelerator ecosystem evolves, accelerator nodes are no longer just a count of identical devices. Workload performance depends on the interconnectivity of devices, their relationship to CPUs and NICs, and node groupings into larger domains like racks and TPU slices.

Our goal is to give Ray an accurate and consistent picture of this structure across vendors and platforms. With that picture, Ray’s scheduler can place tasks and actors on the right hardware, and users can see what their cluster is made of and how it is connected.

Our initial priorities are:

  • Common hardware interfaces. Define vendor-neutral interfaces for labeling hardware, representing its architecture, and describing its specifications, so applications and libraries can target capabilities instead of writing vendor-specific code. This includes a consistent way to identify accelerator SKUs, including new ones at launch. It also includes a documented extension point and checklist for vendors adding a new accelerator.
  • Hardened discovery. Strengthen Ray’s discovery mechanism, with clear ownership for each accelerator’s integration, and back it with the CI coverage described in the previous section. Discovery should capture the topology and architecture of the hardware, not just the type and number of devices.
  • Platform and cloud integration. Work with cloud providers and deployment platforms so that discovery reflects the underlying structure wherever a cluster runs. Some of this information, such as which rack or slice a node belongs to, is only available from the platform, not from the node itself.
  • Hardware visibility. Provide ways to view the accelerators in a cluster and how they are connected, alongside accelerator metrics on the Ray dashboard. This lets users confirm that Ray sees their hardware correctly and understand where their work was placed. It also gives contributors a way to verify new integrations.
  • Clear user guides. Document how Ray discovers and represents hardware, and how to use that information when placing work. Good guides help both application developers and the coding agents that increasingly write Ray code for them.

LinkNetworking and I/O Transport

Moving data between accelerators is often just as important as running computation on the accelerator itself. Modern AI workloads, like large scale reinforcement learning, require moving large model weight tensors across devices and nodes from training to inference workers. Historically, Ray’s object store was built for CPU data, meaning accelerator tensors had to be copied to host memory, serialized, and sent over standard host networking before reaching another device.

To avoid that bottleneck, Ray Direct Transport (RDT) was introduced to enable actors to pass references to tensors through Ray while transferring the actual data directly between devices and using high performance transports like UCX and RDMA. Our goal is to make high-speed, direct data transfer work reliably across different accelerators, frameworks, and network fabrics, while keeping Ray’s familiar programming model.

Our initial priorities are:

  • Broad transport integrations. Support a wider range of accelerators, frameworks, and interconnects in RDT so Ray can select the fastest path between Actors, whether over intra-slice TPU ICI, same-node NVLink, or cross-node GPUDirect RDMA.
  • Transport lifecycle and recovery. Ensure each hardware transport cleanly handles initialization, teardown, and error recovery on real devices, so RDT works reliably as actors scale or restart in dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning and disaggregated serving.
  • Validated recipes and observability. Enable cloud and hardware providers to publish validated deployment configurations, benchmark high-throughput workloads, and surface clear diagnostics and transport metrics.

LinkScope

While core scheduling and placement logic remain in Ray Core, SIG Accelerator is responsible for defining the plug-in interfaces, CI testing, and maturity tiers for accelerators in Ray. Hardware vendors and cloud providers contribute and maintain their own device plugins, transports, and day-zero support for new SKUs, while framework authors and ML practitioners ground our roadmap in real workload needs.

LinkGet Involved

Whether you are building a new accelerator integration, running large-scale training or inference on Ray, or providing cloud and CI infrastructure, we invite you to get involved!

  • Join the conversation on the Ray Slack.
  • Attend our community meetings to discuss proposals, review roadmap priorities, and share workload feedback.
  • Check out open accelerator related issues and PRs on Github and contribute upstream.

Table of contents

  • Development and Testing Infra
  • Hardware-aware Scheduling
  • Networking and I/O Transport
  • Scope
  • Get Involved

item.title: [Hugging Face] TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier tha…
item.description: Full title: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

Published October 19, 2026

Update on GitHub

13

Régis Pierrard

regisss

Simon Pagezy

pagezyhf

Michael Benayoun

michaelbenayoun

Jingya Huang

Jingya

Alvaro Moran

tengomucho

David Corvoysier

dacorvo

Jeff Boudier

jeffboudier

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

New backend, native interface in HF libraries

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Transformers

Inference

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

import os

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch_neuronx  # noqa: F401
from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig

MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B"
MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024
PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512

dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron")
world_size = dist.get_world_size()

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size),
    device_mesh=DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(world_size))),
).eval()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
if tokenizer.pad_token is None:
    tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
tokenizer.padding_side = "left"

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "The future of AI is"}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    padding=True,
    tokenizer_kwargs={"pad_to_multiple_of": PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE},
    return_tensors="pt",
)

generation_config = GenerationConfig(
    max_new_tokens=128,
    do_sample=False,
    use_cache=True,
    pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
    eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
    cache_implementation="static",
    max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN,
    prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE,
    compile_config=CompileConfig(backend="neuron", fullgraph=False, dynamic=False),
)

with torch.no_grad():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        inputs["input_ids"],
        attention_mask=inputs["attention_mask"],
        generation_config=generation_config,
    )

if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    prompt_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
    print(tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0, prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens=True))

Training

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

import os

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig

from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser


def main(script_args, training_args, model_args):
    # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660)
    torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False

    training_args.model_init_kwargs = {
        "revision": model_args.model_revision,
        "trust_remote_code": training_args.trust_remote_code,
        "attn_implementation": model_args.attn_implementation,
        "dtype": model_args.dtype,
        "device_map": None,
    }
    if int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", "1")) > 1:
        # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded
        training_args.model_init_kwargs["distributed_config"] = DistributedConfig(
            tp_size=int(os.environ.get("TP_SIZE", "1")),
            fsdp_size=int(os.environ.get("FSDP_SIZE", "1")),
        )

    # Prepare dataset
    train_dataset = load_dataset(
        script_args.dataset_name,
        name=script_args.dataset_config,
        split=script_args.dataset_train_split,
    )
    # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset.
    train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns(["messages"])

    # Training
    trainer = SFTTrainer(
        model=model_args.model_name_or_path,
        args=training_args,
        train_dataset=train_dataset,
    )

    trainer.train()
    trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir)
    trainer.end()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig))
    script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config()
    main(script_args, training_args, model_args)

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

  • Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes.
  • torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure.
  • Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1.

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \
    --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
    --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \
    --dataset_train_split train_sft \
    --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \
    --dtype bfloat16 \
    --max_length 2048 \
    --packing true \
    --packing_strategy wrapped \
    --learning_rate 2e-5 \
    --warmup_steps 0.03 \
    --num_train_epochs 1 \
    --logging_steps 2 \
    --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \
    --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \
    --save_only_model true \
    --torch_compile true

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Diffusers

Inference

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP
from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig

# Distributed devices initialization
dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron") # TP
dev = torch.neuron.current_device()
mesh = DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(8))) # TP=8

# Pipeline initialization
model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1"
transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained(
    model,
    subfolder="transformer",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP
)
pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    model,
    transformer=transformer,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
pipe.vae.to(dev)
pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

# Image generation
emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt="A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting", device="cpu")  # text encoder stays on CPU
image = pipe(
    prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev),
    prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None,
    height=1024,
    width=1024,
    num_inference_steps=40,
    generator=torch.Generator("cpu").manual_seed(0), # same noise on every rank
).images[0]
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    image.save("out.png")

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Kernels

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Acknowledgments

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bed…
item.description: Full title: Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models, on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, where the model is available.

Whether you call Claude through Boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or through the Messages API and the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now receive schema-compliant JSON responses that conform to a defined structure. You no longer need custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing.

Practical applications

With structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock, you can automate reliable, schema-compliant tasks across industries. Examples include extracting every required field from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, parsing clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR), and enriching product catalogs with consistent, validated results. You can also analyze contracts for key terms, parties, and obligations, or power intelligent support ticket routing where intents, sentiments, and entities always match your application’s data model.

What changes with structured outputs on Amazon Bedrock

Structured outputs use constrained decoding to enforce your JSON schema during token generation, not after the fact. The model doesn’t produce tokens that would violate your schema. This changes output formatting from probabilistic to deterministic.

Two complementary mechanisms are now available on both Amazon Bedrock endpoints:

FeaturePurposeUse case
JSON Schema output formatControl the model’s response structureData extraction, report generation, API responses
Strict tool useValidate tool parameters against schemasAgentic workflows, function calling, multi-step automation

What this means for you

Each response is a valid JSON, so you no longer encounter JSON.parse() errors or parsing exceptions. Responses are also type safe: field types are enforced, and required fields are always present. Because outputs always conform to your schema, you don’t need retries to handle schema violations, making your integration more reliable. Structured outputs also constrains responses to only the fields your schema defines, which reduces output token count and can lower inference costs for high-volume workloads. These properties make structured outputs production ready, so you can deploy at scale without additional schema-validation code.

Supported models and availability

Structured outputs works with batch inference, so you can process large volumes of requests asynchronously while still receiving schema-compliant outputs. On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, it also works with cross-Region inference, so you can use it across AWS Regions without additional setup. If you need responses in real time, you can stream structured responses as typed events.

How it works

When you make a request with a JSON schema, here’s what happens behind the scenes:

  • Schema validation – Amazon Bedrock validates your JSON schema against the supported JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 subset.
  • Grammar compilation – For new schemas, Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact (the first request might take slightly longer).
  • Caching – Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours, making subsequent requests faster.
  • Constrained generation – The model generates tokens that produce valid JSON matching your schema.

Performance considerations

For performance, the first request with a new schema might take longer because Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact before generation begins. After that initial compilation, subsequent requests using the same schema run with minimal overhead because the compiled grammar is cached. This cache is scoped to your account and lasts for 24 hours from first access. Changing the structure of your JSON schema invalidates the cache and triggers a fresh compilation, while changing only the name or description fields leaves the cached grammar intact.

Getting started: Structured outputs with the InvokeModel API (bedrock-runtime)

The InvokeModel API takes the Anthropic-native request body, so the schema goes in output_config.format as a JSON object rather than a JSON string. The following example shows how to extract the structured lead data from a customer email using boto3 with an Anthropic Claude model:

Python

import boto3
import json

REGION = "us-east-1" # Choose your preferred region
bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(service_name="bedrock-runtime", region_name=REGION)

# Define the JSON schema for structured output
schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "name": {"type": "string", "description": "Customer name"},
        "email": {"type": "string", "description": "Customer email address"},
        "plan_interest": {"type": "string", "description": "Product plan of interest"},
        "demo_requested": {"type": "boolean", "description": "Whether a demo was requested"}
    },
    "required": ["name", "email", "plan_interest", "demo_requested"],
    "additionalProperties": False
}

# Make a request with structured outputs via the InvokeModel API
# (reusing the schema defined for the Converse example)
response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(
    modelId="global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5",
    body=json.dumps({
        "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31",
        "max_tokens": 512,
        "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": (
                "Paulo Santos (paulo@example.com) is interested in our Enterprise plan "
                "and wants to schedule a demo for next Tuesday at 2pm."
            )}
        ],
        "output_config": {"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": schema}}
    })
)

body = json.loads(response["body"].read())

# Check the stop reason before parsing
if body["stop_reason"] == "end_turn":
    result_text = next(b["text"] for b in body["content"] if b["type"] == "text")
    print(json.dumps(json.loads(result_text), indent=2))
elif body["stop_reason"] == "max_tokens":
    print("Response truncated: increase max_tokens and retry.")

JSON

{
    "name": "Paulo Santos",
    "email": "paulo@example.com",
    "plan_interest": "Enterprise",
    "demo_requested": true
}

The response conforms to your schema. No additional validation is required.

For additional API usage examples, including the Messages API, see the accompanying sample notebook.

Strict tool use for agentic workflows

Amazon Bedrock Mantle is designed for agentic applications with server-side tools, background inference, and stateful conversations. With strict tool use on the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now guarantee that tool parameters match your input schema exactly. The following example shows how to define a tool with strict schema enforcement:

Import json
from anthropic import AnthropicBedrockMantle

# Reusing the client created in the Messages API example
client = AnthropicBedrockMantle(aws_region="us-east-1")

message = client.messages.create(
    model="anthropic.claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather like in San Francisco?"}],
    tools=[
        {
            "name": "get_weather",
            "description": "Get the current weather for a specified location",
            "strict": True,
            "input_schema": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "location": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "The city and state, e.g., San Francisco, CA"
                    },
                    "unit": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                        "description": "Temperature unit"
                    }
                },
                "required": ["location", "unit"],
                "additionalProperties": False
            }
        }
    ]
)

#Tool inputs conform to the schema
for block in message.content:
    if block.type == "tool_use":
        print(f"Tool: {block.name}")
        print(f"Input: {json.dumps(block.input, indent=2)}")

Setting strict: true constrains the model’s tool input to match your schema exactly. The location field is always a string, and the unit field is always either celsius or fahrenheit. The model can’t add fields outside your schema, so the tool input contains only what your schema specifies.

This is especially valuable for agentic use cases on Amazon Bedrock Mantle, where models orchestrate multi-step workflows with server-side tools like web search and code interpreter.

Top use cases for Claude structured outputs

Structured outputs reduce error-handling complexity the most in three common patterns:

  • Data extraction: Extract fields from invoices, contracts, email, and transcripts into JSON that always matches your schema, ready to load into databases or customer relationship management (CRM) systems.
  • Reliable agent tool calls: Validate tool arguments against their schemas at generation time, so multi-step agent workflows run without failures from malformed input.
  • Classification at scale: Classify tickets, leads, or content by intent, priority, and sentiment for routing, moderation, and evaluation.

Claude Haiku 5.5 reliably handles quick and repetitive workloads such as summaries, compactions, database queries, and classification requests. The following example shows how to classify and route incoming data using the Invoke API and Haiku 5.5:

import boto3
import json

REGION = "us-east-1" # Choose your preferred region
bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(service_name="bedrock-runtime", region_name=REGION)

# Classification schema: enums restrict output to a fixed set of labels
schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "category": {
            "type": "string",
            "enum": ["billing", "technical", "account", "sales", "other"],
            "description": "Primary ticket category"
        },
        "priority": {
            "type": "string",
            "enum": ["low", "medium", "high", "urgent"],
            "description": "Urgency based on business impact"
        },
        "sentiment": {
            "type": "string",
            "enum": ["positive", "neutral", "negative"],
            "description": "Customer sentiment"
        },
        "escalate": {"type": "boolean", "description": "Whether a human should review immediately"},
        "reason": {"type": "string", "description": "One-sentence justification for the classification"}
    },
    "required": ["category", "priority", "sentiment", "escalate", "reason"],
    "additionalProperties": False
}

ticket = (
    "Our production API calls have been failing with 500 errors since this morning. "
    "We're losing orders every minute. This is the second outage this month!"
)

# Make a request with structured outputs via the InvokeModel API
response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(
    modelId="global.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5",
    body=json.dumps({
        "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31",
        "max_tokens": 512,
        "system": "You are a support ticket classifier. Classify the ticket accurately.",
        "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Classify this support ticket:\n\n{ticket}"}
        ],
        "output_config": {"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": schema}}
    })
)

body = json.loads(response["body"].read())

# Check the stop reason before parsing
if body["stop_reason"] == "end_turn":
    result_text = next(b["text"] for b in body["content"] if b["type"] == "text")
    result = json.loads(result_text)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
    # Route the ticket based on the guaranteed-valid labels
    if result["escalate"]:
        print(f"Escalating to on-call: {result['category']} / {result['priority']}")
elif body["stop_reason"] == "max_tokens":
    print("Response truncated: increase max_tokens and retry.")

Requirements and best practices

To use structured outputs effectively on Amazon Bedrock, follow these guidelines:

  • Set additionalProperties: false on all objects: This is required for structured outputs to work. Without it, your schema won’t be accepted.
  • Use descriptive field names and descriptions: Models use property names and descriptions to understand what data to extract. Clear names like customer_email outperform generic names like field1.
  • Use enum for constrained values: When a field has a limited set of valid values, use enum to constrain options.
  • Start basic, then add complexity: Begin with the minimum required fields and add complexity incrementally. Basic schemas compile faster, are easier to debug, and keep your request payload lean because the schema counts toward the Converse API payload size.
  • Reuse schemas to benefit from caching: Structure your application to reuse schemas across requests. The 24-hour grammar cache improves performance for repeated queries.
  • Check the stop reason in every response: Two scenarios can produce non-conforming responses: refusals (when the model declines for safety reasons) and token limits (when max_tokens is reached before completing). Handle both cases in your code.
  • Test with realistic data before deployment: Validate your schemas against production-representative inputs. Edge cases in real data often reveal schema design issues.

For additional best practices and schema design recommendations, see Structured outputs in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

Supported JSON Schema features

  • All basic types: object, array, string, integer, number, boolean, null.
  • enum (strings, numbers, booleans, or nulls only).
  • const, anyOf, allOf (with limitations).
  • $ref, $def, and definitions (internal references only).
  • String formats: date-time, time, date, duration, email, hostname, uri, ipv4, ipv6, uuid.
  • Array minItems (only values 0 and 1).

Not supported

These keywords are accepted by the API but are not enforced during generation. A request that includes them returns a successful response, and the model can still return values that violate them. Validate these constraints in your application rather than relying on the schema to enforce them.

  • Recursive schemas.
  • External $ref references.
  • Numerical constraints (minimum, maximum, multipleOf).
  • String constraints (minLength, maxLength).
  • additionalProperties set to anything other than false.

Conclusion

Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock provides the reliability that production AI applications require. It is available now on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints. By combining JSON Schema output format and strict tool use, you can build data pipelines that need no additional validation. You can also create reliable agentic workflows and production AI applications without custom parsing or retry logic.

Structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock is now generally available. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation and explore our sample notebook.

What workflows could validated, schema-compliant JSON improve in your organization? Share your feedback and questions in the comments.

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new A…
item.description: Full title: Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new AWS experience
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new AWS experience

Today, we’re excited to announce that new Amazon SageMaker AI customers can now land inside a fully configured Amazon SageMaker Studio environment in only a few steps after signing up for AWS. You can use a sign-in method that you already have, such as Amazon, Apple, GitHub, Google, or an email address. You don’t need to set up an advanced AWS account, enter a credit card (for most customers), or configure an environment manually. New customers also receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including model customization, training jobs, Studio notebooks, and endpoint deployments.

This post follows on from our previous post, From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in One Click, which introduced deep links from Hugging Face model pages directly into SageMaker Studio workflows. Earlier this year, we also sped up Studio environment creation time from 2 minutes to about 20 seconds and pre-configured model customization permissions in every new Studio domain. Together, these changes removed much of the friction after a developer reached Studio. One major hurdle remained before they got there: creating an AWS account. New customers had to verify an email address, enter contact information, verify a phone number, provide payment details, and select a support plan before they could start building. For individual developers and small startup teams used to signing in and building within a few minutes, that was still a significant barrier.

What’s new

With this launch, SageMaker Studio is now integrated with the updated AWS sign-in and sign-up experience, which introduces new options for creating and managing AWS accounts along with simplified collaboration. New customers can create an account using an identity that they already have and start building in SageMaker Studio right away.

New sign-in experience

New customers can now sign up using their Google, GitHub, Apple, or Amazon account, or with an email address, in 2–3 steps. You don’t need to complete the advanced AWS account sign-up, verify a phone number, or enter a credit card (for most customers):

Figure 1: The Sign up for AWS page with social sign-on options

After you sign up, SageMaker AI automatically creates your Studio environment in about 20 seconds. You then land on the page that matches where you started. For example, you might discover and select a model from Hugging Face for deployment through Deploy on SageMaker AI. Studio then opens the Deployment page with the model pre-configured for endpoint creation:

Figure 2: Deploying a Hugging Face model on Amazon SageMaker AI

Figure 3: Configuring endpoint settings in SageMaker Studio

Up to $200 in Free Tier credits, no credit card required for most customers

New customers receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including endpoint deployments, model customization, Studio notebooks, and model training. You also have the chance to earn an additional $100 worth of credits. Credits are applied automatically to your usage, and you receive an email notification as you approach your limit. The Free Tier period ends after 6 months or when you’ve used all your credits, whichever comes first. At that point, resource usage stops automatically, so you won’t be surprised by unexpected charges. You can upgrade to a paid plan at any time by adding payment details.

Built on the foundations of previous launches

New environments created through the new sign-in experience include the improvements from earlier launches. Permissions for model customization, training, evaluation, and deployment are pre-configured, so you don’t need to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles.
