Before Stage 8, mean time to detect (MTTD) was days to weeks. After Stage 8, it is under four hours, and the first signal is a CloudWatch alarm with an AgentCore trace attached.

Stage 9: The Feedback Loop. Continuous improvement

This stage turns observations into actions. The system compounds quality over time. We use AgentCore optimization, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to close the loop.

  • System prompt recommendation: Analyzes agent traces and generates a data driven optimized system prompt that improves performance on the target evaluator. The solution uses failure patterns and adds specific behavioral instructions.
  • Tool description recommendation: Analyzes agent traces and generates sharpened tool descriptions that reduce tool selection confusion. Particularly when an agent selects the wrong tool for ambiguous requests.

Let’s look at an example:

AgentCore optimization in action
What to improve on: Target evaluator: hallucination: model reproducing hardcoded values from few-shot examples verbatim in unrelated contexts.
Why this happened: Few-shot examples contain real dollar amounts and customer names (for example, “$4.2M”, “Acme Corp”) that the model memorizes and leaks into unrelated queries.
How to fix: Replace hardcoded values in few-shot examples with generic placeholders (for example, $[AMOUNT], [CUSTOMER_NAME]) so the model learns response structure without memorizing specific data points.
Impact and result: Fix applied. Pure hallucination occurrences dropped from 138 to under 52 per 10,000 responses, and overall grounding rate improved from 93 percent to 96 percent.

AgentCore optimization uses recommendations to produce data driven system prompt and tool descriptions changes based on real agent traces and a target evaluator. AgentCore optimization builds on AgentCore Evaluations . Low-scoring traces are promoted into the golden set as permanent regression guards so each failure does not reach users twice.

Quality: ToolRetrieval precisionRetrieved context contains the information needed% retrievals with relevant context
Quality: ToolSQL generation accuracyData Insights Agent generates correct SQL% correct result sets (deterministic)
Quality: ToolTool pass rate% of tool calls returning a valid response% success per tool
Quality: Multi-agentEnd-to-end accuracy pass rateFull orchestration path produces a correct response% of scenarios passing all evaluators
Quality: Multi-agentRouting accuracyOrchestrator routes to the correct sub-agent(s)% correct routing (deterministic)
Quality: Multi-agentSynthesis faithfulnessSub-agent outputs combined without distortionLLM-as-judge score across agent boundaries
Quality: Multi-agentContext propagation accuracyContext passed between agents is correct and complete% traces with no context loss
SafetyGuardrail block rate% of requests blocked at input or outputPer 1,000 requests
SafetyInput / Output violation rate% of queries or responses flagged as policy-violating% of total requests / responses
SafetyGuardrail latencyLatency overhead added by guardrail checksp99 (target: under 50ms)
PerformanceEnd-to-end latencyQuery received to response deliveredp50, p90, p99
PerformancePer sub-agent / tool latencyPer sub-agent and per tool executionp50, p90, p99 independently
PerformanceLatency regression rateCI runs that breach the Stage 1 latency threshold% of CI runs
CostCost per queryTotal token cost per end-to-end user requestInput + output tokens × price
CostCost per successful responseCost per query divided by pass ratePenalizes costly failures
CostAvg tool calls per queryReasoning efficiency. Rising calls signal degradationAverage per query
Ops controlMTTD / MTTRTime to detect and remediate, per failure classHours (MTTD target: under 4h)
Ops controlAutomation detection rateIncidents detected by evaluation compared to user complaints% (target: above 95%)
Ops controlAlarm false positive rateAlarms not corresponding to real degradation% of total alarms

Conclusion

The impact of the nine-stage agent evaluation framework was concrete and measurable. Quality regressions that previously took days or weeks to surface, and usually arrived through a seller complaint, are now caught in under four hours by automated evaluation. Deployment decisions that once relied on subjective judgment now require every evaluator to pass a quantitative threshold. Prompt iteration cycles fell from days to minutes. Safety moved from periodic audits to 100 percent guardrail coverage on every request. Latency regressions are caught at the CI gate before they reach production. Cost surprises that once appeared weeks later in billing are now evaluated at Stage two and enforced by the quality gate before a change ships. And “something in the agent pipeline” became one click from a CloudWatch alarm to a full agent execution trace with every reasoning step visible.

The broader lesson is one the industry has learned before. DevOps taught us that shipping code without automated testing is reckless. MLOps taught us that deploying models without monitoring is dangerous. AgentOps teaches us the same thing about AI agents: operating them without continuous, multi-level evaluation is flying blind.

The nine-stage framework described here is not specific to sales intelligence agents. Team deploying multi-agent systems that reason, call sub-agents, tools, and synthesize responses will face these same questions across the same lifecycle. Your failure taxonomy will look different. Your golden set will reflect your domain. Your evaluator stack will be tuned to your users. What stays constant is the principle: evaluation is not a final QA step. It is the operating system of the agent itself, continuously measured, automatically defended, and improved with every interaction.

If you are building production agents and want to bring this kind of evaluation discipline to your system, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations gives you the platform to do it: on-demand evaluation for experiments, batch evaluation for continuous monitoring, online evaluation for live traffic, built-in and customized evaluators, dataset evaluation(in public preview), CloudWatch integration, and the AgentCore optimization features recommendations and A/B tests to close the feedback loop. Start with Stage one, define what good looks like for your agent, and let the framework do the rest.

Ready to start? See Evaluate agent performance in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation. And if you’re building production agents and want to talk through how to apply this framework to your system, we’re happy to help. Reach out to us directly or through your AWS account team.

To learn more about Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, see Evaluate agent performance in the AWS documentation. For a technical introduction, read Build reliable AI agents with AgentCore Evaluations. To see how we built the Performance Insights Agent, read How AWS SMGS uses an AI-powered conversational assistant to transform business management with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. To learn about AgentCore recommendation and optimization, read AgentCore optimization: Improve agent quality loop with recommendations and A/B tests​

Acknowledgement

We extend our sincere gratitude to our executive sponsors and mentors whose vision and guidance made this initiative possible: Damien Forthomme, Manager III, Applied Science; Akhand Singh, Head of Data Engineering; Sujit Narapareddy, Director AWS Insights; Monica Jain, Sr. Product Manager – Tech and Norman Braddock, Senior Manager of AI Product Management at AWS; Muhammad Umar Javed, Applied Scientist III, L6.

item.description: Full title: Introducing Reflection Beam: an open-weight model for agentic coding on AWS
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing Reflection Beam: an open-weight model for agentic coding on AWS

Reflection AI introduced Beam, an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon tasks such as maintaining code, using tools, interpreting results, and completing multi-step workflows. The open-weight release gives developers and researchers control over the runtime, deployment environment, and customization process.

In this post, we explain Reflection’s vision and show how you can deploy Beam on AWS. Start with an Amazon SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint for a fully managed path. When you need Kubernetes-native control over distributed GPU infrastructure, use Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with JumpStart, SGLang, or vLLM. We also explain how Beam’s 501 billion total parameters shape checkpoint storage, weight memory, sharding, and parallelism, while its 23 billion active parameters influence per-token compute.

At launch, Beam is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio).

Reflection’s vision for open intelligence

Reflection’s mission is to make intelligence open and accessible to all through open model weights, published research, and open source software. Its full AI stack spans models, core software, production infrastructure, and applications. Beam brings this approach to developers building software engineering and agentic systems.

About Reflection Beam

Beam is a sparse mixture-of-experts model for resolving software issues, modifying code, calling tools, and acting on intermediate results. It has 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active parameters, and Reflection reports an effective context length of 1 million tokens.

Reflection releases Beam’s weights through Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam 1.0 is available in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoint variants. These formats provide different memory footprints and hardware compatibility. You can deploy the model with the AWS managed JumpStart container configuration or inspect and customize the model with SGLang or vLLM in your AWS environment.

Understand the deployment architecture

Choose the serving path that meets your control and scaling requirements.

  • Start with a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint when you want an AWS managed model package, endpoint, and invocation API without operating Kubernetes.
  • Use JumpStart on HyperPod Inference when you want the AWS managed container and model configuration on a HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS).
  • Use SGLang or vLLM on HyperPod Inference when you need to control the serving image, runtime arguments, quantization, or distributed execution.
  • Size the deployment for checkpoint storage, weight memory, KV cache, context length, batching, runtime overhead, and the supported parallelism.
  • Define the expected concurrency and latency targets, then configure replicas, caching, routing, and autoscaling from measured workload behavior.

The JumpStart real-time path packages the model, container, and endpoint behind a managed deployment workflow. The HyperPod path exposes the cluster and serving runtime so that you can control distributed execution, caching, routing, and scaling.

The following diagram shows the components used by the HyperPod path. Beam can be sourced through SageMaker JumpStart, Hugging Face Hub, or an optional Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) mirror. The distributed workers use the AWS managed JumpStart container or a custom SGLang or vLLM runtime.

Figure 1: Distributed Beam deployment with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference

Prerequisites

You need:

  • An AWS account with permissions for your selected SageMaker deployment path and its supporting AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), networking, and storage resources.
  • Access to Beam through SageMaker JumpStart or one of the Beam 1.0 checkpoint repositories on Hugging Face.
  • Acceptance of the model terms, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), and Python 3.11 or later.
  • GPU quota and capacity for a supported Beam configuration.

Plan and obtain GPU capacity

Beam’s 501 billion total parameters require a multi-GPU deployment. BF16 has the largest weight-memory requirement, so plan a multi-node configuration with enough aggregate GPU memory for the weights and runtime overhead. For FP8, use ml.p5.48xlarge with NVIDIA H100 GPUs or ml.p5e.48xlarge and ml.p5en.48xlarge with H200 GPUs. For NVFP4, use ml.p6-b200.48xlarge with NVIDIA B200 GPUs. Confirm that the released checkpoint, runtime, and parallel layout support the selected instance type.

  • Calculate memory for weights, KV cache, and runtime overhead for one replica, then confirm the estimate with a load test.
  • Choose an AWS Region that supports the required accelerated instance.
  • Check the service quota and available capacity for the selected instance type. Use on-demand capacity when available, or use a SageMaker training plan as a short-term reservation for scheduled work.
  • Allow time for image transfer, weight download, shard loading, and runtime initialization.

Path 1: Get started with a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint

Use a JumpStart real-time endpoint first when you want the shortest path from the model catalog to a managed HTTPS endpoint. The sample supports the BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 model IDs through one variant-aware command. Its README and Python file are the source of truth for supported instance types, request schema, deployment command, and cleanup command.

  • Clone the sample repository. git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples.git
  • Enter the SageMaker JumpStart deployment sample directory. cd sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples/01-models/ReflectionAI/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4/
  • Create and activate a Python virtual environment. python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate
  • Install the sample dependency. python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
  • Run the bounded deployment, invocation, and cleanup lifecycle for FP8. python jumpstart_real_time.py \ --variant fp8 \ --endpoint-name reflection-beam-fp8-smoke The command deploys the FP8 endpoint, sends a short request, prints the response, and cleans up the endpoint. Use bf16 or nvfp4 to select another checkpoint variant; NVFP4 is the default when you omit --variant. Use the Python functions in the README when you need to keep an endpoint running.

Path 2: Deploy with SageMaker HyperPod Inference

Use HyperPod Inference when you need Kubernetes-native control over distributed GPU infrastructure. You can use the AWS managed JumpStart container configuration or deploy Beam with SGLang or vLLM. The HyperPod Inference deployment sample README and its configuration files are the source of truth for released manifests, model and image identifiers, supported runtime versions, and commands.

Before you begin, configure kubectl access to an EKS-orchestrated HyperPod cluster with the HyperPod Inference Operator and required add-ons. You also need the cluster virtual private cloud (VPC), subnets, security groups, access to the selected Beam and runtime artifacts, and local NVMe capacity if you enable model caching. Use an isolated Hugging Face access token if the selected repository requires authentication.

Deploy a pinned Beam revision from Hugging Face Hub for development and experimentation. For production deployments and model caching, copy the checkpoint to Amazon S3 or Amazon FSx. HyperPod model and image caching can preload weights onto node-local NVMe storage and pre-pull the serving image.

The HyperPod Inference Gateway provides an OpenAI-compatible interface and routes requests across replicas. HyperPod Inference also supports managed tiered KV caching and intelligent routing. These are among the Amazon SageMaker Inference capabilities introduced in 2026.

The next diagram expands the model preparation and runtime request flow. When model caching is enabled, the Inference Operator warms eligible nodes with the selected weights and serving image. At runtime, the Inference Gateway and Endpoint Picker can direct each request to a suitable JumpStart-managed, SGLang, or vLLM replica.

Figure 2: HyperPod model caching and request routing

Prepare deployment artifacts

Use immutable inputs so that you can reproduce deployment and performance results.

  • Use the JumpStart model release recorded in the deployment sample.
  • Choose the BF16, FP8, or NVFP4 checkpoint for a custom runtime.
  • For a custom runtime, keep the public Beam commit SHA and image digest in the sample release configuration.
  • Mirror the released image into a private Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository only when your cluster cannot pull the upstream image or your organization requires an approved registry.
  • Keep tokens, generated secrets, private model IDs, registry credentials, and unpublished results out of the repository.

Choose a serving path

Start with SageMaker JumpStart unless your workload requires a specific inference runtime or configuration.

Serving pathUse it whenWhat you manage
SageMaker JumpStartYou want an AWS-managed container and model configuration with less runtime maintenance.Select the Beam model version, supported instance type, endpoint configuration, and scaling policy.
SGLang or vLLMYou need a specific inference runtime or configuration, such as custom runtime arguments, parsers, quantization, or parallelism.Pin the supported runtime image, model revision, parser configuration, and distributed execution settings.

Deploy with SageMaker JumpStart

SageMaker JumpStart reduces container integration work while HyperPod retains control over cluster capacity, scaling, and observability.

  • In SageMaker Studio, open the JumpStart model catalog.
  • Under All public models, choose Beam.
  • Choose SageMaker HyperPod as the deployment target.
  • Select the cluster and Kubernetes namespace.
  • Enter an endpoint name, and choose Deploy.
  • Confirm the deployment status before invoking the endpoint with the released JumpStart request schema.

For an infrastructure-as-code workflow, use the released JumpStart configuration in the HyperPod sample. You can inspect the reflection-beam-jumpstart.yaml manifest template before configuring the deployment.

  • Clone the sample repository, and enter the HyperPod Beam directory. git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples.git cd sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples/SageMakerHyperpod/reflection-beam/
  • Create the local configuration files described in the README. cp config/deployment.env.example config/deployment.env cp config/release.env.example config/release.env
  • Validate the JumpStart configuration before changing the cluster. python hyperpod_tool.py \ --config config/deployment.env \ --config config/release.env \ validate jumpstart
  • Deploy the JumpStart configuration. python hyperpod_tool.py \ --config config/deployment.env \ --config config/release.env \ deploy jumpstart \ --timeout-seconds 1800

The helper renders and applies the released JumpStartModel resource without writing populated release values to disk.

Deploy with SGLang or vLLM

Choose SGLang or vLLM when you need direct control over the serving runtime. Before configuring the deployment, inspect the reflection-beam-sglang.yaml manifest template or the reflection-beam-vllm.yaml manifest template. The sample README remains the source of truth for released values and commands.

  • Clone the sample repository. git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples.git
  • Enter the HyperPod Beam directory. cd sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples/SageMakerHyperpod/reflection-beam/
  • Create the local configuration files described in the README. cp config/deployment.env.example config/deployment.env cp config/release.env.example config/release.env
  • Validate the selected configuration before changing the cluster. python hyperpod_tool.py \ --config config/deployment.env \ --config config/release.env \ validate sglang
  • Deploy Beam, and wait for a terminal deployment state. python hyperpod_tool.py \ --config config/deployment.env \ --config config/release.env \ deploy sglang \ --timeout-seconds 1800 Replace sglang with vllm to use vLLM. The helper validates the selected settings, applies the rendered manifest without writing release values to disk, waits with a fixed timeout, and prints diagnostics if deployment fails.

Invoke Beam

Invoke JumpStart endpoints with the released model request schema. For SGLang or vLLM, use the bounded smoke test included in the HyperPod sample.

Invoke the deployed endpoint

  • Install the sample client dependency. python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
  • Run a private health check and short request with the recommended starting sampling settings. python hyperpod_tool.py \ --config config/deployment.env \ smoke sglang \ --prompt "List three checks for a healthy model deployment." \ --temperature 1.0 \ --top-p 0.7 Replace sglang with vllm for a vLLM deployment. The helper selects a ready worker, opens a temporary port-forward, checks endpoint health, sends the request, and closes the port-forward.

The response resembles the following:

1. Confirm that the endpoint reports ready.
2. Send a short inference request.
3. Review the service logs for startup errors.

For an authenticated Inference Gateway, use the bearer-token procedure in the HyperPod sample README. Keep credentials out of source code, manifests, and command history.

Measure and tune performance

  • Test each serving path with repeated, representative coding and tool-use requests at the expected concurrency.
  • Record the Beam model version, image digest, instance type, precision, context length, parallelism, serving arguments, cache state, and test repetitions.
  • Measure request success rate, p50 and p95 time to first token, time per output token, end-to-end latency, and aggregate output tokens per second.
  • Tune batch size, KV cache allocation, replica count, autoscaling, and model and image caching from those results.
  • Recheck output quality after changing precision or quantization.

Clean up

Delete resources when you finish testing to avoid ongoing charges.

  • For a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint, follow the cleanup instructions in the SageMaker JumpStart deployment sample README.
  • For JumpStart, SGLang, or vLLM on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference, follow the cleanup instructions in the HyperPod Inference deployment sample README.
  • Delete a dedicated HyperPod or Amazon EKS cluster created for the walkthrough.
  • Delete unused cached weights, mirrored artifacts, load balancers, log groups, temporary IAM roles, and captured inference data.

Conclusion

Reflection Beam gives developers an open-weight model designed for agentic coding and multi-step tasks. Start with a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint for a fully managed deployment. Use SageMaker HyperPod Inference with JumpStart when you need Kubernetes-native infrastructure control without managing the serving container, or choose SGLang or vLLM when you need a custom runtime.

Use the SageMaker JumpStart deployment sample or the HyperPod Inference deployment sample, then follow the instructions.

To learn more about Reflection AI and its vision for open intelligence, visit Reflection AI and read Introducing Beam.

Resources

  • Reflection Beam checkpoint variants: BF16, FP8, and NVFP4
  • SageMaker JumpStart deployment sample
  • HyperPod Inference deployment samples with JumpStart, vLLM, and SGLang
  • Deploy foundation models from SageMaker JumpStart to HyperPod Inference
  • Amazon SageMaker Inference 2026 year-to-date launches in review

About the authors

item.title: [DeepInfra] Open-Weight Model Licenses: What to Check Before You Ship
item.content:encoded:
Open-Weight Model Licenses: What to Check Before You Ship

Published on 2026.10.16 by DeepInfra

Do enterprise workloads always need the most capable AI model available? More companies are questioning this assumption as the costs of frontier models increase, and many routine tasks do not require more advanced capabilities.

Due to this, open-weight models are moving beyond developer experimentation and becoming a part of production AI workloads. But deploying open-weight models raises legal and governance concerns.

Licensing approaches vary from permissive licenses to custom commercial terms. There are restrictions that can create compliance risks or limit deployment options.

So, which license terms should enterprises check before choosing an open-weight model for production? In this article, we explore how open-weight model licenses are diverging in 2026, five key licensing checks, and the risks enterprises should consider before deployment.

Open Weights Don’t Mean Unrestricted Use

A model’s weights are the numerical parameters learned during training that determine its responses. Open-weight models make these weights available for download. This does not include the training code or data. And downloading these weights does not automatically grant rights to modify or commercially deploy the model.

Open-weight models are different from open-source software as they can be subject to custom licensing terms that govern how developers can use and deploy them. These licenses specify the permissions and conditions for commercial use, fine-tuning, redistribution, and hosted inference.

Open-weight models can also require integration with software platforms to run and manage them. Their licenses may impose additional conditions related to intellectual property (IP), attribution, and downstream deployment.

How Open-Weight Model Licenses Are Diverging in 2026

Most major new open-weight models now use permissive licenses, such as MIT or Apache 2.0 licenses. More restrictive terms are concentrated among a smaller group of vendors and older models that remain widely deployed.

This shift has followed several major model releases. OpenAI’s gpt-oss, Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4, DeepSeek V4, and Meta’s Muse Glimmer use either the Apache 2.0 or MIT license. Some recent releases, including Gemma 4 and Muse Glimmer, have just switched to the Apache 2.0 license, reflecting a move toward standardized, permissive licensing.

Some Chinese AI labs use custom licenses that include additional commercial conditions. For example, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 requires certain large model-hosting companies to sign a separate agreement. Similarly, Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 mandates that qualifying businesses undergo a security review before using the model commercially.

Licenses vary across model families, which include related models released by the same developer in different versions or sizes. Qwen3 uses the Apache 2.0 license, whereas older Qwen2.5 releases retain a custom license agreement that includes a monthly active user threshold for commercial products and services.

Some licenses also impose conditions on hosted services. Kimi K3’s license requires a separate agreement when a Model as a Service (MaaS) business exceeds $20 million in aggregate revenue over any consecutive 12-month period. GLM-5.3’s license requires a security review when a MaaS operator’s aggregate revenue exceeds $10 billion over the same period.

Commercial and usage restrictions vary by model. For instance, MiniMax M3 has revenue-based conditions for commercial use and specifies prohibited use cases. Licensing terms vary from basic attribution or notice requirements to more conditions on commercial use and deployment.

The table below shows how many recent major open-weight models use permissive licenses, while others retain custom terms with additional commercial restrictions:

ModelLicenseLicense familyRelease dateCommercial useKey restrictions
Qwen2.5-72BQwen License AgreementCustom / scale-basedSep 2024ConditionalAuthorization above 100M monthly active users (MAU); derived-model attribution
Qwen3Apache 2.0PermissiveApr 2025YesCopyright and license notices
gpt-ossApache 2.0 + usage policyPermissiveAug 2025YesLicense notices; compliance with applicable law
Mistral 3Apache 2.0PermissiveDec 2025YesCopyright and license notices
Gemma 4Apache 2.0PermissiveApr 2026YesCopyright and license notices
DeepSeek V4MITPermissiveApr 2026YesCopyright and license notices
MiniMax M3MiniMax Community LicenseCustom / scale-basedJun 2026ConditionalAttribution and notification; authorization above $20M annual revenue; prohibited uses
Kimi K3Kimi K3 LicenseCustom / scale-basedJul 2026ConditionalMaaS agreement above $20M annual revenue; display rules above 100M MAU or $20M monthly revenue
Muse GlimmerApache 2.0PermissiveAug 2026YesCopyright and license notices
GLM-5.3GLM-5.3 LicenseCustom / scale-based2026ConditionalMaaS security review above $10B annual revenue

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Please consult legal counsel to review the applicable license when deploying a model.

Five Licensing Checks Before You Ship a Model

Understanding license terms becomes more important as open-weight models gain more adoption. This includes custom licensing terms and IP exposure as well as governance obligations and evolving regulations.

These conditions affect whether a model meets an organization’s needs. Reviewing them early enables teams to identify licensing obligations and potential risks before shipping a model.

The following five checks highlight the conditions to evaluate before shipping a model:

Commercial Use and Revenue Thresholds

Check whether a model’s license permits commercial use without additional approval or imposes revenue and user-count thresholds. The Kimi K3 license imposes additional requirements on certain commercial deployments.

These conditions can restrict how organizations use a model when they exceed specific revenue thresholds. Companies also need to check whether these thresholds apply to individual products or aggregate revenue across the organization and its affiliates as this distinction can affect licensing obligations.

Hosted Inference and MaaS Restrictions

Some models’ licenses impose additional conditions on hosted inference or third-party access through an API. Kimi K3’s license requires qualifying MaaS businesses to sign a separate agreement if their aggregate revenue with affiliates exceeds $20 million over a consecutive 12-month period.

So, before offering Kimi K3 to customers, a company needs to understand how its service is classified under the license. The way it provides the model to users defines whether an additional agreement is required.

Fine-Tuning and Modification

Check if the license allows you to fine-tune or modify the model and deploy that version. And look for any conditions that apply. The Kimi K3 license explicitly allows users to modify the model and create derivative works.

Permission to fine-tune a model does not necessarily imply that all uses of the modified model are unrestricted. For example, Kimi K3’s license imposes additional conditions on certain commercial uses of the model and its derivatives, including qualifying Model-as-a-Service businesses.

Redistribution, Attribution, and License Notices

Check the requirements for distributing a model or its derivatives, including license copies and attribution notices. The Kimi K3 license requires its copyright and permission notices to be included in all copies or substantial portions of the software.

Distributors must include a copy of the license and mark modified files under the Apache 2.0 license. They must also retain the required notices in distributed derivative works. Companies must review the specific model license before redistributing it or its modifications.

Prohibited Uses and Additional Conditions

Check if your intended use case is within the model’s permitted uses and complies with its restrictions. Google’s Gemma restricts certain uses involving sensitive personal information and automated decisions that affect individuals’ rights.

These restrictions can influence whether a model is appropriate for a planned application, especially in sensitive areas such as healthcare and finance. Review the applicable prohibited usage policy and the model’s license to confirm that both permit the intended deployment.

Why Model Licensing Becomes an Enterprise Risk

Open-weight model deployments can involve more legal considerations than traditional software procurement or hosted AI services. They can create risks that extend beyond the license terms. IP uncertainty, security responsibilities, contractual protections, and changing regulatory requirements can further complicate enterprise deployment.

Several factors show how these risks can affect enterprise deployment:

  • Licensing obligations can sometimes conflict with business goals. Some licenses impose copyleft provisions that contradict an organization’s goal of keeping proprietary software confidential.
  • Model access does not ensure IP protection. Permission to use a model does not guarantee that it is free from third-party IP claims. Warranty disclaimers and liability limits may leave enterprises with limited recourse against the provider.
  • Contractual protections vary depending on the deployment approach. Managed inference providers may offer support and security controls. But enterprises must check the contractual terms to understand how their data is handled and who is responsible if something goes wrong.
  • Evolving regulations add uncertainty. Changes to AI regulations and data transfer rules change where enterprises can deploy models and which providers they can use. An enterprise might deploy a model or choose a provider only to discover that regulatory requirements restrict that deployment in a particular jurisdiction.

How DeepInfra Supports Enterprise AI Inference

Enterprises selecting an inference platform must consider not only model access and infrastructure but also how providers manage their data.

Routing platforms send requests to various model providers where data-handling and retention practices can vary. Enterprises using these platforms may need to evaluate the policies of multiple providers.

DeepInfra takes an integrated approach to inference infrastructure by combining GPU infrastructure with purpose built networking and inference optimized software as a unified inference platform. This frees enterprises from managing the stack themselves or evaluating multiple model providers.

DeepInfra’s optimization stack combines inference software, open-weight models, and GPU infrastructure. | Source

DeepInfra’s terms limit customer data retention to the duration necessary for processing requests with specified exceptions for operational metadata and legal or security needs. It also holds SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certifications and also allows customers to enter into a separate data processing agreement (DPA).

These measures cover important aspects of enterprise AI inference but do not replace the need for a license review. Companies still need to verify that a model’s license permits the intended use and evaluate the contractual terms associated with its deployment.

Final Thoughts

Open weights provide access to model parameters but do not grant universal commercial rights. Reviewing license terms before deployment will help identify restrictions that may impact future business plans and avoid surprises.

DeepInfra lets enterprises deploy models in production without requiring them to manage the entire underlying infrastructure. It provides a broad model catalog and owns and operates its own GPU infrastructure. Its terms also include a zero-data-retention policy, with specified exceptions.

Explore DeepInfra’s models to compare available models and identify options for your workloads.

Should this request go to the fast cheap model or the expensive one? Is this tool call safe to execute? Is the task actually finished, or does the agent think it is finished? […]</p>

It is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 480 billion total parameters and 35 billion active parameters per inference, enabling high performance […]</p>

item.title: [InceptionLabs] Mercury 2 Named to TIME's Best Inventions of 2026Read story
item.content:encoded:
Today, TIME named Mercury 2 to its Best Inventions of 2026 list in the Artificial Intelligence category. Mercury 2 is the first diffusion LLM built to reason, and we're proud to see our new approach to language model architecture recognized alongside this year's other honorees. See the full list.

Thank you to our customers, our investors, and the team that spent years betting that language models don't have to write one word at a time.

A new foundation

AI now runs inside coding assistants, voice agents, search systems, copilots, and agentic workflows that take repeated actions inside larger loops. Each step adds delay, and reasoning adds more.

The cause is architectural. Nearly every LLM in production today is autoregressive. It generates text one token at a time, so the more a model thinks, the longer users wait and the more each completed task costs. The industry has spent billions working around that limit with specialized chips, optimized serving stacks, and model compression. These workarounds help, but they leave the underlying architecture in place.

Diffusion, applied to language

Mercury 2 is built on diffusion, the approach behind modern image and video generation, now applied to language. Instead of committing one token at a time like a typewriter, it works like an editor: it generates many tokens in parallel and refines them over several passes.

Mercury 2 generates over 1,000 tokens per second, more than 5x faster than leading speed-optimized LLMs.

Speed is only part of the story. As AI infrastructure costs climb and data centers strain to keep up with demand, every token carries a cost in compute, electricity, and cooling water. Autoregressive generation leaves GPUs waiting on memory much of the time. Mercury 2 gives them the dense parallel work they were designed for, producing more output per GPU cycle and per unit of energy on widely available NVIDIA GPUs.

What's come since: Mercury 2.5, Mercury Voice, Mercury Router, Mercury Decide

Mercury 2 launched in February. In September, we followed it with Mercury 2.5, our most capable production model yet. It is a significant step up in quality over Mercury 2, with the same low-latency, low-cost serving profile. Mercury Voice is our dLLM optimized for voice agents, delivering time-to-first-token under 170ms, Mercury Router understands user prompts and routes tasks to the best models according to quality, speed, and cost, and Mercury Decide is a System One decision model,that is rated by ValsAI as more accurate and more affordable than Jev.

Coming soon, we'll be releasing our most capable model to date. If you're interested, please reach out for early access.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Code Review is now generally available
item.content:encoded:
Code Review is out of research preview and available to Claude Team and Enterprise organizations.

Eligible Claude Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Code Review credits by January 15, 2027. Credits expire 30 days after you claim them. Terms apply.

What's new in Code Review

Coding agents keep increasing the pace at which teams write code, and the review bottleneck hasn't eased. For general availability, we made Code Review faster, better at finding the bugs that matter, and easier to tune to each of your repositories.

Since we released the research preview, Code Review has gotten sharper, catching more of the bugs that would otherwise reach production. We also run Code Review on pull requests at Anthropic, which shows us where reviews slow our own engineers down. Teams using Code Review during the preview told us the rest: it was catching real issues before a human reviewer looked at the PR, but they wanted reviews that were quieter, sized to each change, and faster. Here’s what we shipped:

  • Speed: Most reviews now finish about 3x faster (~20 minutes down to 6-10 minutes) compared to during preview.
  • Quality: Find more of the bugs that matter, with clear, concise findings that state the problem, what triggers it, and the fix in a few sentences.
  • Flexibility: Admins choose Quick, Standard or Deep for each repository, so routine codebases get a quick pass and the most critical ones get a deep review. Every level delivers high-quality reviews.

Get started

Code Review is now generally available for Team and Enterprise plans.

  • For admins: Enable Code Review in your Claude Code settings, install the GitHub App, and select repositories you’d like to run reviews on.
  • For developers: Once enabled, reviews run automatically on new PRs. No configuration needed.

Explore the docs for more information.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] An update on independent evaluators
item.content:encoded:
Last month, we committed to stronger independent, third-party assessment of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.

METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on several reviews of our Risk Reports. We’re also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face.

Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.

Why we work with independent evaluators

As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.

To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:

  • Expertise in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as alignment faking.
  • Independence: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.
  • Enough access to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.
  • Freedom to publish observations and assessments of a model or a process.

Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.

For the AI industry, this is a step toward robust safety oversight. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.

What we mean by “employee-like access”

We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.1

METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into predefined categories such as reproducing confidential IP. (Anthropic ultimately decides what information does and does not fall into these categories, although METR reserves the right to make certain statements about the level of access and information it received.)2

Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.

Our other evaluator partnerships

We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.

We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.

In the first tier, evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.

In the second tier, evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.

The third tier is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.

SecureBio is in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our August Risk Report, after completing and publishing a pilot review of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access.3

With Accenture and Faculty, we're working toward an ambitious partnership that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.

We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.

Footnotes

01Because these evaluators (like bank examiners) may also work with other companies, we exercise caution around the possibility of inadvertent leaks. Information about architectures presents a high risk of inadvertent leaks, and its relevance to risk assessment is typically low. When it is highly relevant, we will generally seek to share it, though this will require explicit internal approvals.

02Updated on October 16 to clarify METR's current project terms with Anthropic.

03Updated on October 15 to clarify SecureBio's current project terms with Anthropic.

item.title: [Mistral AI] Introducing Timestral
item.content:encoded:
Introducing Timestral

October 15, 2026

By Mistral

7 min read

Copy url to clipboardCopied

Thinking

Summary

Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.

Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.

Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.

Time Series Foundation Models (TSFM)

Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.

Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.

Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.

Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.

Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.

Benchmark Results

We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.

GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.

TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.

fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.

Family of models optimised for every specification

Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.

Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.

Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.

An industrial example

Consider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.

Multivariate forecasting. A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.

Probabilistic forecasting. A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.

Categorical covariates. Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.

Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.

From Model to System

Timestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.

In the plant, that could look like this:

  • Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.
  • When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.
  • The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.
  • The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.

The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.

Key technical contributions

Several ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.

  • Decoupled Horizon Forecasting. Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.
  • Covariate-aware attention. Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.
  • Synthetic-first data. The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.
  • Two-stage training. Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.

A model that can be adapted

Public benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.

For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through Mistral Forge, the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:

  • Zero-shot inference out of the box.
  • Architectural extensions, such as domain-specific covariates.
  • Fine-tuning on proprietary data, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.
  • Control over the training data, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.

The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.

What’s next

We have published a GitHub repository so you can run Timestral on your own data. A technical report with the full results will follow. For more specialised forecasting problems, or to collaborate on research, please reach out to us.
